h1: What HR teams should know when hiring for brewery roles
title: Hiring for Brewery Roles: A Guide for HR | Craft Beer School
desc: What HR teams should know before hiring brewers, cellar staff and quality roles: the skills that matter, safety, qualifications and interview tips.
teaser: A brewer's CV can look thin on paper and be brilliant on the floor. Here is how HR can tell the difference.
standfirst: Hiring for a brewery is unlike hiring for an office. The work is physical, hot, wet and safety critical. It runs on shifts and depends on skills that rarely appear neatly on a CV. This guide helps HR teams hire well for brewing, cellar, packaging and quality roles.
sections: Know the roles before you write the advert

Brewery jobs are often lumped together as "brewer". In practice there are several distinct roles:

  • Head brewer or brewing manager. Owns recipes, quality, schedule and the team.
  • Brewer or shift brewer. Runs brew days: milling, mashing, boiling, transfers and cleaning.
  • Cellar operator. Fermentation, yeast handling, filtration, tank cleaning and transfers.
  • Packaging operator. Runs bottling, canning or kegging lines.
  • Quality or lab technician. Tests beer, runs microbiology and sensory checks, keeps records.
  • Maintenance technician. Keeps pumps, chillers, boilers and fillers running.

Each needs a different profile. Our guide to jobs in a brewery describes the day-to-day work. For staffing levels see brewery staffing.

Across most production roles the same traits separate good hires from poor ones:

  • Cleaning discipline. Most of brewing is cleaning and sanitising. Someone who is careless here will cost the business batches.
  • Safety awareness. Breweries have hot liquids, caustic and acid chemicals, pressurised vessels, carbon dioxide and confined spaces.
  • Record keeping. Brew logs, excise registers and quality records must be accurate. In many states excise compliance depends on them.
  • Mechanical sense. Pumps, valves, gaskets and heat exchangers need someone comfortable with tools.
  • Sensory ability. For brewers and quality staff, being able to taste and describe beer reliably.

Passion for beer is common among applicants. It is a fine start, not a qualification.

Brewing qualifications range widely. Some candidates have degrees in brewing science, food technology, microbiology, biotechnology or chemical engineering. Others hold short professional certificates or diplomas, including international ones. Many skilled brewers learned on the job, sometimes after years of homebrewing.

A degree shows the science. It does not prove the person can run a brew day. Experience shows practice. It does not prove they understand why things go wrong. For senior roles look for both, or a clear plan to fill the gap. Our guide to hiring your first head brewer goes deeper on the most important hire.
Interview questions that reveal real skill

• Walk me through how you clean and sanitise a fermenter. What chemicals, at what strength and what temperature?
  • Tell me about a batch that went wrong. How did you find the cause?
  • What does diacetyl taste like and how do you prevent it?
  • How do you enter a tank safely?
  • What records do you keep on a brew day?

Good candidates answer with specifics: a caustic strength, a temperature, a test they used. Weak candidates answer in generalities. Involve your head brewer in the technical round. HR cannot judge those answers alone. Nor should it have to.

A practical trial, a paid shift on the floor or a tasting test where the candidate identifies faults in spiked samples, tells you more than any interview.

Be honest in the advert about shifts, weekend work during peak season, heat, lifting and wet conditions. Indian summers make brewhouses and packaging halls hot, physically demanding places. Hiring someone who expected an air-conditioned lab leads to early resignations.

Make sure safety induction, personal protective equipment and training are in place before the first day. A brewery's safety culture is set by what happens in a new joiner's first week.

Onboarding matters as much as selection. A new cellar operator should shadow an experienced colleague for their first weeks, work through written procedures for cleaning and transfers and sign off each task before doing it alone. Build a short checklist with the head brewer for every production role. It protects the new joiner, the beer and the business. It also gives HR a clear record of who is trained on what, which helps with audits and shift planning.
Building the team, not filling a seat

Small breweries often rely on one or two people who know everything. That is fragile. When you hire, ask how this person's skills cover a gap and who they will train or be trained by. Written standard procedures, cross-training and a clear path from operator to brewer help keep good people.

HR teams that understand the brewery floor hire better. Spending a day there before running a hiring round is the best preparation we know of.
faqs: Does a brewer need a brewing degree?
Not always. Many skilled brewers learned on the job. For senior roles, look for both scientific understanding and practical experience.
HR should run the process, but a head brewer or senior brewer should lead the technical round and any practical trial.
What safety training do new brewery staff need?
Induction on chemicals, hot liquids, pressure vessels, carbon dioxide and confined spaces, plus the right protective equipment, before they work on the floor.
